name: Ross chin shaper and ear-correcting device

card.summary: Victorian clip-type devices from London perfumer Alexander Ross, sold to reshape the chin and press protruding ears closer to the head.
card.aka: Ross chin machine, Ross ear machine
card.note: Historical product; dates and prices for these two devices are not documented.

quick.overview:
Alexander Ross was a London perfumer who sold beauty products such as depilatories, hair-curling fluid and complexion pills. After his nose machine of 1871, a Ross Jnr. produced similar devices for the chin and for protruding ears.

The appeal was a more balanced face with no surgery: a refined chin and ears sitting flat to the head. The nose machine, the best documented, was a boxwood clamp described as shaping soft cartilage with an hour of daily wear.
quick.how: The devices were worn for set periods; the related nose machine was advertised for one hour a day. Specific instructions for the chin and ear devices are not documented.
quick.risks: No details of harm are recorded for the chin and ear devices. Contemporary press treated the nose machine mostly as a curiosity.

lead: Alexander Ross was a London perfumer who also sold depilatories, hair curling fluid, complexion pills, skin-tightening lotion and a hair restorer [1]. He is best known for the nose machine launched in late 1871 and advertised in 1872 [1].
Ross Jnr. later produced a similar device for changing the chin shape and another for correcting protruding ears [1]. No prices, addresses or dates for these two are given in the source.

chain: Clip-type device worn on chin or ears
Steady pressure applied for set periods
Claimed refined chin or flatter ears
angle.text: Ross advertised pressure devices to reshape the nose, chin and ears without surgery. Those claims were the vendor's.

paras: The nose machine was advertised in The Examiner on 10 February 1872 at 10s. 6d. from 248 High Holborn, with a pamphlet for two stamps [1]. A mid-1890s description in the Hampshire Chronicle called it a small boxwood clamp joined by two screws [1]. Critics and humorists, including the Pall Mall Gazette and Punch, mocked it, and it never gained much credibility [1].
Ross Jnr. later made similar devices for the chin and for protruding ears [1]. Corrective ear caps for children, such as the Claxton cap, are a separate later product.
